why: Every marketing interview starts here: how people discover, choose and come back to a product, and how you would measure it. With these basics you can read any campaign, talk to any team and pick the right channel.
outcome: explain the funnel and the main channels, define a target and a message, compute the core metrics (CTR, CPL, CAC, ROAS, LTV), tag links with UTM parameters and write a campaign plan.

lessons.title: What digital marketing does: the funnel
text: Marketing brings the right people to a product and helps them choose it. Online, every step leaves data, so you can see where people drop out and fix it.

The funnel describes the steps: awareness (they hear of you), consideration (they compare), conversion (they buy or sign up), retention (they come back) and advocacy (they recommend you). Each step has its own goals, channels and metrics.
points: A funnel is read from top to bottom: each step keeps only part of the previous one.
Most growth comes from fixing the biggest drop, not from adding more visitors.
Retention matters: keeping a customer usually costs less than finding a new one.
B2B funnels add steps between lead and sale: qualified lead, meeting, proposal.

lessons.title: Customers and positioning
text: Before choosing channels, know who you speak to. A persona is a short, evidence-based portrait of a typical buyer: their job, the problem they want solved, how they decide and where they look for information.

Positioning says why your product is the best choice for that person, compared with the alternatives they really consider. It becomes the value proposition: one clear sentence about the result they get.
points: Build personas from interviews, reviews and sales calls, not from imagination.
Describe the job the customer wants done and what stops them today.
A value proposition names a result, for whom, and how it differs from the alternative.
One campaign, one audience, one message: mixing them weakens all three.

lessons.title: The channels: owned, earned and paid
text: Owned media are the channels you control: website, blog, newsletter, app, social accounts. Earned media are what others say: press, reviews, shares, word of mouth. Paid media are what you buy: search ads, social ads, display, sponsoring.
Each channel matches a funnel step and a budget. Search captures people who already look for a solution; social and display create demand; e-mail and the product keep customers active.
points: SEO and content: slow to start, cheap over time.
Search ads: fast, measurable, but you pay for every click.
Social ads: precise targeting by profile and interests, good for awareness and demand.
E-mail: the best return for people who already know you, if they agreed to receive it.

lessons.title: Copy that converts
text: Good marketing copy is clear before it is clever. It speaks to one reader, names their problem in their words, shows the result and asks for one action.

Classic structures help: AIDA (attention, interest, desire, action) for ads and landing pages, PAS (problem, agitation, solution) for e-mails and posts. Test headlines: they decide whether the rest is read.
points: One page, one goal, one call to action.
Benefits before features: what changes for the reader.
Proof makes claims believable: numbers, reviews, logos, case studies.
Write for skimming: short sentences, subheadings, lists.

lessons.title: The metrics every marketer uses
text: Metrics turn activity into decisions. Click-through rate shows whether an ad interests people; conversion rate shows whether the page convinces them; cost per lead and customer acquisition cost show what growth costs.

Return on ad spend (ROAS) compares revenue with ad cost; lifetime value (LTV) estimates what a customer brings over time. Comparing LTV with CAC tells you how much you can afford to pay for a customer.
points: Always state the formula and the period: a metric without definition starts arguments.
Vanity metrics (likes, impressions) rarely prove value on their own.
A common rule of thumb: LTV around three times CAC or more.
Look at the trend and the comparison, not one number.

example.code:
CTR             = clicks / impressions
Conversion rate = conversions / visits (or clicks)
CPC             = cost / clicks
CPL             = cost / leads
CAC             = sales and marketing cost / new customers
ROAS            = revenue from ads / ad cost
LTV             = average order value x orders per year x years as a customer (x margin)
example.note: Write these definitions in every report so everyone reads the numbers the same way.

lessons.title: Tracking links with UTM parameters
text: Analytics tools need to know where each visit comes from. UTM parameters are tags you add to a link: source (who sends the visit), medium (the type of channel), campaign (the campaign name), and optionally term and content.
Without them, a newsletter or a social post often shows up as 'direct' or 'referral' traffic and its results are lost. With a naming convention shared by the team, reports stay clean.
points: utm_source = newsletter, google, linkedin…; utm_medium = email, cpc, social…
Use lowercase and the same spelling every time: 'Email' and 'email' become two channels.
Never put UTM parameters on internal links of your own site: they restart the session.
Keep a shared sheet of the links and names you use.

example.note: Ad platforms such as Google Ads can tag clicks automatically (auto-tagging); UTM parameters are for the rest.

lessons.title: Planning a campaign
text: A campaign plan answers six questions: what result we want (a SMART objective: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound), for whom, with what message, on which channels, with which budget, and how we will measure it.
Plan the measurement before launch: UTM links, conversion tracking, a baseline to compare with and a review date. After the campaign, write what worked, what did not and what you will test next.
points: Start from the business goal, then the marketing goal, then the channel.
Split the budget so you can compare and move money to what works.
Decide in advance what result would make you stop or scale.
Keep a log of tests and results: it becomes your team’s memory.

example.code:
Objective : +300 qualified leads in Q2 (from 180 in Q1), cost per lead under 25 EUR
Audience  : HR managers in companies of 50-500 people, France
Message   : "Cut onboarding time in half" + customer case study
Channels  : LinkedIn Ads (60 %), Google Ads on brand + 3 problem keywords (30 %), newsletter (10 %)
Budget    : 7,500 EUR over 12 weeks
Measure   : leads by channel (UTM), CPL weekly, lead-to-meeting rate monthly
example.note: A one-page plan like this is often all a manager needs to approve a campaign.

items: People buy, sign up or ask for a demo
Cost to win one new customer
Revenue from ads divided by ad cost
What a customer brings over the whole relationship
Channels you control: site, newsletter, blog
Press, reviews, shares, word of mouth
Search ads, social ads, display, sponsoring
Evidence-based portrait of a typical buyer

pitfalls: Choosing channels before knowing the audience and the goal.
Reporting impressions and likes as if they proved business results.
Launching without conversion tracking or UTM links, then guessing what worked.
Talking about features instead of the result the customer gets.
Changing several things at once, so nobody knows what made the difference.

exercises.q: A campaign had 20,000 impressions, 400 clicks and 20 sign-ups for a cost of 600 €. What is the cost per lead?
exercises.answer: Cost per lead = cost / leads = 600 / 20 = 30 €. (1.50 € is the cost per click: 600 / 400.) The click-through rate is 400 / 20,000 = 2 % and the conversion rate 20 / 400 = 5 %.

exercises.q: Put the steps of the marketing funnel in order, from first contact to recommendation.
exercises.answer: People first hear of you, then compare, then buy or sign up, then stay and come back, and finally recommend you. Each step needs its own content and metric.

exercises.q: Match each metric with what it tells you.
pairs: Whether people who see the ad click it
Whether visitors do the action you want
What one new customer costs to acquire
Revenue earned for each euro of advertising
What a customer brings over the whole relationship
exercises.answer: CTR is about the ad, conversion rate about the page or offer, CAC and ROAS about cost and return, LTV about the long-term value of a customer.

exercises.q: Complete this newsletter link so analytics knows the source and the type of channel.
exercises.answer: utm_source names who sends the visit (newsletter) and utm_medium the type of channel (email). Keep values lowercase and consistent.

exercises.q: Sort these channels into owned, paid and earned media.
exercises.answer: Owned media are yours to control, paid media are bought, earned media are what others say about you: the most trusted and the hardest to get.

exercises.q: An online training company wants more sign-ups for its free trial. Write a SMART objective and the three metrics you would follow every week.
exercises.answer: Example: “Go from 400 to 600 free-trial sign-ups per month by the end of June, keeping the cost per sign-up under 12 €.” Weekly metrics: sign-ups by channel (from UTM links), cost per sign-up, and trial-to-paid conversion (to check the new sign-ups are good ones).

interview.q: How would you explain the marketing funnel to someone outside marketing?
interview.a: It is the path from not knowing a product to buying and recommending it: awareness, consideration, conversion, retention, advocacy. At each step some people drop out; marketing finds the biggest drop and fixes it, and measures each step with its own metric.

interview.q: What is the difference between CAC and CPL?
interview.a: Cost per lead counts what it costs to get a contact; customer acquisition cost counts what it costs to win a paying customer, including the leads that never buy and often sales costs. A low CPL with poor lead quality can give a high CAC.

They tell the analytics tool where each visit comes from, so results can be attributed to the right channel and campaign. Without them, e-mails and posts often appear as direct traffic and their impact is lost.

interview.q: How do you choose channels for a new product?
interview.a: From the audience and the goal: where the target already looks for solutions, whether demand exists (search) or must be created (social, content), the budget and the time available. I start with two or three channels, measure, and move budget to what works.

interview.q: What makes a good landing page?
interview.a: One audience, one goal and one call to action; a headline that states the result; benefits before features; proof such as reviews or numbers; a short form; fast loading on mobile. Then test the headline and the offer.
